claims.text: Controlled annealing at selected temperatures and times can steer phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Annealing can promote controlled precipitation of thermodynamically stable phases.
Annealing can suppress undesired metastable or residual solid-solution states.
The as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy is predominantly a metastable solid solution.
The as-cast alloy may have a heterogeneous microstructure.
Appropriately selected annealing temperatures activate diffusion and phase-transformation kinetics.
An inert annealing atmosphere prevents oxidation.
Precise control of annealing temperature and duration can fine-tune phase stability.
Grain boundaries and intragranular defects act as diffusion pathways.
Grain boundaries and intragranular defects facilitate the nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
Thermal energy supplied during annealing enhances atomic diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion enables nucleation of more thermodynamically stable ordered phases.
Annealing reduces the metastability of the as-cast solid solution.
Controlling transformation kinetics can manage phase size, phase distribution, and microstructural stability.
Controlled annealing will produce a higher volume fraction of desired stable precipitate phases than the as-cast state.
Controlled annealing will improve phase uniformity relative to the as-cast state.
The annealed microstructure may have enhanced mechanical properties relative to the as-cast state.
Rapid solidification in the as-cast condition produces a metastable solid solution with an inhomogeneous phase distribution.
Annealing below the effective temperature window provides insufficient diffusion for the proposed phase evolution.
Annealing above the effective temperature window may cause excessive or deleterious phase coarsening.
